blocks.text: 2.2 Aviation market assessment
Airlines run Cape Town's full routes for yield rather than volume and withdraw seats in winter, so new seats must be won route by route.
What was asked

The aviation work answered the inception brief to review current airlift and planned route development as part of route to market (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p15). MIDAS Aviation set itself four questions (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Introduction"). How well has the Western Cape developed new air services, and how does that record compare with similar markets? What challenges and opportunities do the next five years hold, and which emergent markets matter?
The agreed report structure assigns this work to SLA Annexure B clause 1.1.1.2. [Clause wording to be checked against the signed Annexure B.]
What was done

MIDAS measured scheduled seats and estimated bookings for every Cape Town route. Bookings come from the airlines' global distribution systems, weighted to the full market, and so "will not always reconcile exactly with airport published data" (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The South African Market"). The latest annual booking set runs to November 2025 ("Seasonality").

Cape Town was compared with eight secondary airports chosen for peripheral geography and inbound tourism: Calgary, Christchurch, Edinburgh, Keflavik, Larnaca, Marrakech, Santiago and Valencia (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "International Comparisons"). The report is a Word file without page numbers, so it is cited here by section.

The Infrastructure Report of July 2026 assessed the physical side of access: Cape Town International, George, the proposed Cape Winelands airport and the secondary airfields (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p101 to p109). Its airport findings are summarised here because they set the ceiling the airlines fly into; its spatial findings sit in 2.5.
Findings that survived into the tree

**1. Cape Town has already won its routes.** Twenty-nine international routes serve the airport in 2026, and Cape Town added 17 mainline international services between 2015 and 2025, more than Santiago (14), Valencia (12) or Calgary (8) (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Executive Summary"; "International Comparisons"). The body of the report counts fourteen new routes since 2014, a difference this report logs. Cape Town's share of South Africa's international capacity rose from 10% in 2010 to 25% ("The Capetown Market").

MIDAS calls the result "a 'what next' moment" (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "In Conclusion"). Tactical gains remain in frequency and aircraft size. The next phase needs a strategy that "looks for long-term gains rather than short-term wins" ("In Conclusion").

The new carriers lean towards Africa. Seven of the twelve carriers that launched Cape Town services since 2014 fly to African points, and the largest by seats are Airlink and Ethiopian Airlines (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The Capetown Market").

blocks.caption: Twelve carriers have launched Cape Town services since 2014, seven of them to African points.
blocks.source: MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The Capetown Market" (carriers launched since 2014, 2026 scheduled seats).
rows: Dar es Salaam and Victoria Falls

blocks.text: **2. The network runs through hubs, and none of it reaches Asia.** The seven largest international markets are all hubs, with 2.7 million seats in 2026 against 2.0 million in 2019 (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The Capetown Market"). Western Europe holds 38% of international capacity, the Middle East 23%, Southern Africa 17%, Eastern Africa 14% and North America 6% ("The Capetown Market").

Most passengers on those hub routes are connecting. Emirates' connecting share is "above 80% annually" and Qatar Airways' nine in ten (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). MIDAS records "the absence of any direct capacity to any of the Asian markets", and the Diagnostic counts one airline serving Cape Town from Asia against ten from Africa ("The Capetown Market"; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p35).

**3. The routes that exist are full.** Eleven of the 27 international routes in the load table ran above 80% in the year to November 2025, led by Newark at 88.6%, Atlanta at 84.3% and Frankfurt and London Heathrow at 83.0% (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). Sixteen ran at 75% or more, the count the agreed structure attributes to the 80% line (computed from the same table).

The printed network total is 76.0% on 3,816,797 seats, though the 27 listed rows sum to 75.0% (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality", computed). Cape Town's 79% average load factor is the highest of South Africa's five largest airports, against about 70% nationally, 75% for Africa and 84% globally ("The South African Market").

blocks.caption: Eleven of Cape Town's 27 international routes ran above 80% in the year to November 2025, and sixteen at 75% or more.
blocks.source: MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality" (international route load-factor table: estimated bookings divided by capacity, bookings for the twelve months to November 2025). Routes above 80% highlighted; the eleven routes below 75% are not shown.

blocks.text: **4. Airlines raise fares before they add seats.** MIDAS expects that "rather than increase capacity carriers will seek to increase revenues via higher selling fares rather than add new services", which "will frustrate that desire for increased visitors" (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "In Conclusion"). The report carries no fare data, so the claim rests on the author's judgement of airline behaviour.

**5. Winter seats are withdrawn.** June carried 6.4% of Cape Town's 2025 international seats and December 10.8%, with May to September at 6.9% each (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). Connecting traffic is "especially critical in the low season" ("Executive Summary"), which ties the winter schedule to the hub carriers' own priorities.

blocks.caption: Airlines schedule 10.8% of Cape Town's annual international seats in December and 6.4% in June.
blocks.source: MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality" (Capetown international capacity by month, 2025, printed data labels).

blocks.text: **6. Regional routes run full and can take more capacity.** Luanda ran at 86.2% and 83.4% on its two airports, Maputo 83.3%, Gaborone 82.3%, Mauritius 81.8% and Harare 81.3%, and MIDAS names all five markets for further capacity (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "Seasonality"). Domestically, Cape Town to Durban runs at 90.0% and "warrants" more seats; other domestic routes sit between 70% and 80% ("Seasonality").

**7. India and China are long-term, government-led prizes.** About 71,000 Indian travellers reached Cape Town indirectly in 2025, half from Mumbai, with Addis Ababa and Dubai carrying 81% of them; direct service is "unlikely before 2030" (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The Indian Market Opportunity"; "Executive Summary"). China sent about 29,600, and its routes are "frequently an extension of government-to-government relations", with Guangzhou and China Southern the likeliest start ("The Chinese Market Opportunity").

MIDAS recommends early relationships between Wesgro, the Indian carriers and Indian government authorities, and treats China as a long-term investment in awareness and indirect volume before any non-stop service (MIDAS Aviation Market Assessment, Mar 2026, "The Indian Market Opportunity"; "The Chinese Market Opportunity"). Australia (61,000 indirect travellers) and Saudi Arabia (137,000 passengers, with Riyadh Air's planned hub) are the next markets on its list ("The Australian Market Opportunity"; "The Saudi Arabian Market Opportunity").

**8. The airport, not the airlines, sets the outer limit.** Cape Town International's single runway has no parallel taxiway and caps movements at about 30 an hour, and two of the airport's seven parts are already full (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p101, p102). The R6.39bn runway relocation adds about 40% more movements an hour but completes around 2033, and relief across the airport lands from about 2032 (p103).

The alternatives arrive sooner but carry less. George handled 911,000 passengers in 2025, above its design limit, and a R310m terminal expansion doubles it to about 2 million by 2028 (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p104, p105). Cape Winelands Airport targets first passengers in 2028 on an R8bn phase one but has no firm airline (p106). In the report's words, "the certain fix is the latest, and the earliest big-capacity option is the least certain" (p109).

blocks.title: What this means for the tree
paras: **Rewords FA07, Win direct routes and add seats on full routes.** Eleven routes above 80%, fares before seats and a runway that binds until about 2032 (findings 3, 4 and 8). The structure's "16 of 27 above 80%" is corrected to eleven.
**Supports FA02, Create green-season demand with MICE and events.** Winter seats fall to 6.4% of the year in June (finding 5).
**Rewords FA04, Convert India and China hub traffic.** No direct Asian route before 2030; conversion runs through the hubs (findings 2 and 7).
**Validates FA05, Increase yield in mature markets.** The mature long-haul routes are the fullest (finding 3).
**Validates FA06, Build a regional foundation (Africa).** Five regional routes above 80% and named for more capacity (finding 6).

**Supports FA16, Align institutional stakeholders across all three tiers, and FA19, Lead removal of infrastructure, visa and safety deficits.** Chinese routes follow government-to-government agreements and airport capacity sits with ACSA (findings 7 and 8).
